hook.question: Python's list.append feels instant, yet an array can't count on growing in place. So where does the new item go?
paragraphs: An array is a block of memory bought in one piece, and whatever sits right after it may already belong to something else. So when 4 items fill a block of 4 and you call append, there is no room next door.
Yet you can append a million items in a loop without waiting. Something must happen when the block is full. What, and why doesn't it slow everything down?
hook.aha: The list moves to a new block twice as big and copies everything across once. That copy costs as much as the list is long, but it buys that many free slots, so the next pushes are a single write each. Added up, the copying comes to less than 2 extra steps per push: amortised O(1).

metaphor: Picture a family in a flat where you can't knock through the walls. When the family grows and every room is taken, they don't squeeze in. They rent a flat twice as big, carry everything across in one trip, and hand back the old keys.
The move is a hassle, but it buys a lot of spare rooms. The next several arrivals each just take a free room, so the family doesn't move again for a long time.
mentalModel.click: Moving everyone costs as much as the family is big, but it buys that many spare rooms, so the next pushes cost nothing extra.

glossary.definition: How many slots hold a real value right now. The next push writes at index size.
How many slots the block has in total. Size can never be bigger than capacity.
How much bigger the new block is. Doubling is a factor of 2. Real libraries use values like 1.5 or 2, and any constant above 1 keeps pushes amortised O(1).
Moving to a new block: allocate it, copy every element across, free the old one. It costs O(size).
Cost averaged over a whole run of operations. One push might copy everything, but n pushes together cost O(n), so the average push is O(1).
After a reallocation the elements live at new addresses. A pointer, reference or iterator into the old block now dangles, and using it is a bug (undefined behaviour in C++).
A policy for giving memory back, such as halving the block once size falls to a quarter of capacity. It is optional: std::vector and Java's ArrayList don't do it on their own.

mentalModel.definition: A dynamic array (std::vector in C++, ArrayList in Java, list in Python) keeps its elements in one contiguous block and tracks two numbers: size, how many slots are in use, and capacity, how many slots the block has. push_back writes at index size. If size equals capacity it first allocates a larger block, usually a constant factor such as 2 times the capacity, copies the elements across and releases the old block. Access by index stays O(1) and push_back is amortised O(1). Inserting or erasing in the middle is still O(n), because the elements after it must shift.

useWhen: You build a list as you go and don't know how long it will end up.
You read or change items by position, and mostly add or remove at the end.
The problem says to collect, build or return a list whose length is unknown until you finish.
You need a stack: push and pop at the back.
notWhen: You insert or delete in the middle or at the front all the time. Every change shifts everything after it, so look at linked lists or queues.
You look things up by value, like a name or an id. A hash map finds them without scanning.
You know the exact size up front and it never changes. A plain array, or one reserve call, avoids all the growing.

quiz.problem: Read a log file line by line and keep every line that contains ERROR. You can't tell how many there will be, and afterwards you want to read them by position.
quiz.explanation: A plain array needs its size up front. A vector grows as you append and still reads any position in O(1).

quiz.problem: A weather app stores exactly 365 daily temperatures, never more and never fewer, and reads day 200 again and again.
quiz.explanation: The size is fixed and known, so there is no growth to manage. A vector would work, but a plain array is the simpler tool.

quiz.problem: Count how many times each word appears in a document.
quiz.explanation: You look things up by word, not by position. A hash map goes straight to the right bucket, while a vector would have to scan.

quiz.problem: A sensor appends a reading every second all day. Later you must jump straight to reading number 5,000.
quiz.explanation: Appending at the end is amortised O(1) and reading by position is O(1). A linked list would have to follow 5,000 links to get there.

quiz.problem: Splice a new item into the middle of a very long chain, at a spot you already hold, many thousands of times.
quiz.explanation: In a vector every middle insert shifts all the later elements, which is O(n). A linked list only rewires two links.

pseudocode.text: data = an empty array of the starting capacity; size = 0; copies = 0
allocate a new array, twice as big (at least 1)
copy data[0 .. size - 1] across, one by one
data = the new array; capacity doubles; the old one is freed

template.time: O(1) amortised per push (O(n) for the push that resizes)
notes: A push into a vector with a free slot is one write. A push into a full one copies everything, O(n). Over n pushes the copies add up to less than 2n, so the average push is a small constant.

Why double instead of adding one slot? Growing by one would copy every element on every push, about n²/2 copies for n pushes. Any constant factor above 1 keeps pushes amortised O(1). A bigger factor wastes more memory, a smaller one copies more often.

Real libraries differ, and versions change. std::vector in libstdc++ and libc++ doubles, MSVC grows by about 1.5, Java's ArrayList by about 1.5, and CPython's list by only about 1.125 plus a few slots. Treat these as ballpark numbers.

Reading and writing by index is O(1), just like an array. Inserting or erasing in the middle is O(n) because later elements shift, and an insert needs the same room check first: if size equals capacity, grow, then shift.

pop_back is O(1): it lowers size and copies nothing, and the old value stays in its slot until something overwrites it. Shrinking is optional. std::vector and Java's ArrayList don't shrink on their own (shrink_to_fit and trimToSize are requests you make), while CPython's list gives memory back once it falls below half full. The quarter rule in the Pop track is a common textbook policy: right after shrinking, the vector is half full, far from both growing and shrinking again.

A reallocation invalidates every pointer, reference and iterator into the old block. If you hold one across a push_back, fetch it again afterwards. If you know roughly how many items are coming, reserve that capacity first and skip the resizes.
A vector can start at capacity 0. The first push has to grow it to 1, so the growth rule needs max(1, 2 × capacity), because 2 × 0 is still 0 and an unguarded vector would never grow.

examples.title: Concatenation of Array
examples.problem: Given an integer array nums of length n, build an array ans of length 2n where ans[i] == nums[i] and ans[i + n] == nums[i] for every 0 <= i < n. Return ans.
approach: The answer has exactly 2n slots and you know n, so ask for all 2n slots once. The array never has to grow.
Copy nums[i] into ans[i] for the first half.
Copy the same nums[i] into ans[i + n] for the second half.
Pushing 2n values into an empty vector would also be O(n) in total, but sizing it up front skips every resize and every copy.

examples.title: Min Stack
examples.problem: Design a stack that supports push, pop, top and retrieving the minimum element, each in constant time.
approach: A stack is just push_back and pop_back on a vector: items.append(val) and items.pop(), amortised O(1) each.
To read the minimum in O(1), keep a second vector, mins, the same length. mins[k] is the smallest value among items[0..k].
On push, append min(val, mins[-1]) to mins, or val itself if mins is empty. On pop, pop both vectors so they stay in step.
top reads items[-1] and getMin reads mins[-1]. Each is a single read.

examples.title: Insert Delete GetRandom O(1)
examples.problem: Implement a set that supports insert(val), remove(val) and getRandom(), each in average O(1). getRandom returns any current element with equal probability.
approach: Keep the values in a vector. getRandom is then a random index from 0 to size - 1. Keep a hash map from each value to its index in the vector, so insert and membership checks are O(1).
insert: if val is already in the map, return false. Otherwise record its index as the current length and append it.
Removing from the middle of a vector would shift everything, O(n). Instead copy the last value into the hole, update that value's index in the map, then pop_back.
A set has no order to preserve, so moving the last value is allowed. Removing from the back is the cheap operation of a vector.

conceptQuiz.question: A vector has size 4 and capacity 4. You push a fifth number. What happens?
options: It writes at index 4 and hopes the memory next door is free
It allocates a bigger array, copies the 4 numbers across, then writes the fifth
It overwrites the first number to make room
It refuses, because a vector can't go past its capacity
conceptQuiz.explanation: There is no free slot, and the block can't be stretched, so the vector moves. After the copy there is room for the fifth number and for several more.

conceptQuiz.question: Why does a vector double its capacity instead of adding one slot at a time?
options: Computers can only allocate blocks whose size is a power of two
Doubling uses less memory than adding one slot
Adding one slot would still be O(1) amortised, but doubling is easier to code
Adding one slot would copy everything on every push, about n²/2 copies for n pushes, while doubling keeps the total under 2n
conceptQuiz.explanation: With +1 growth every push is a full block, so every push copies every element. Doubling makes full blocks rare: each resize buys as many free slots as it copied elements.

conceptQuiz.question: Start with capacity 1 and push 8 numbers, doubling whenever the vector is full. How many copies happen in total?
conceptQuiz.explanation: Growing 1 to 2 copies 1 number, 2 to 4 copies 2, and 4 to 8 copies 4. That is 1 + 2 + 4 = 7, still under 2 × 8 = 16. The ninth push would grow 8 to 16 and copy 8 more.

conceptQuiz.question: A vector with capacity 16 shrinks to capacity 8 as soon as its size falls to 8. What can go wrong?
options: Nothing: half full is the best moment to shrink
Every pop becomes O(n), even when nothing shrinks
Right after shrinking it is completely full, so the next push grows it again and the next pop shrinks it again, copying everything each time
The numbers end up in a different order
conceptQuiz.explanation: Push and pop at the boundary would each trigger a full copy. Shrinking at a quarter leaves the new array half full, far from both limits, so a resize can't repeat straight away.

conceptQuiz.question: You hold a pointer to the first element of a vector, then a push_back triggers a reallocation. What is true about the pointer?
options: It still points at the first element, because elements keep their addresses
It points into the old block, which has been freed, so using it is a bug
It automatically follows the elements to the new block
It now points at the last element
conceptQuiz.explanation: The elements were copied to a new block, so the old address is stale. This is iterator invalidation: after anything that can reallocate, fetch your pointers and iterators again.

practice.title: Plus One
practice.insight: Adding one can carry all the way and turn 999 into 1000, one digit longer than the input. Think about the only case where the answer needs an extra slot.

practice.title: Duplicate Zeros
practice.insight: The array can't grow, so values pushed along fall off the end. Work out where each value lands, and fill from the back so you don't overwrite what you still need.

practice.title: Pascal's Triangle
practice.insight: Build each row by appending to a new vector, using neighbouring numbers of the row above. Row i has exactly i + 1 numbers.

practice.title: Implement Queue using Stacks
practice.insight: Use two vectors as stacks. Moving everything from one to the other costs O(n), but each element moves at most once, so the average cost per operation is O(1): amortised again.

practice.title: Design Browser History
practice.insight: Keep the pages in a vector plus an index for the current page. Visiting a new page throws away everything ahead of the index, which is a run of pop_back calls.

practice.title: Design Circular Queue
practice.insight: This is the opposite of a vector: a fixed capacity that never grows. Indices wrap around with a modulo, so both ends move without shifting anything.

practice.title: Insert Delete GetRandom O(1) - Duplicates allowed
practice.insight: It is the swap-with-last and pop_back trick from the example, but a value can now appear several times, so each value maps to a set of indices instead of one.
